Built from the
deck (`workshop/slides.qmd`), the print page (`workshop/studio-cards.qmd`)
and the schedule CSV. Per-block times get updated after the rehearsal (same
file, new commit, no amend). How this layout was chosen from the three before
it is in `workshop/layout-review.md`. What one learner's day measured is in
`workshop/learner-trace.md`; the minutes below follow it.

The shape of this layout: **the whole path twice, with a studio inside the
first run.** Sprint 1, before lunch, is fast and wide: three questions, one
framed run everyone does the same way, then studio cards on your own
repository with a commit after each, a pull request you merge yourself, and
release v0.1.0, rough on purpose. Sprint 2, after lunch, runs the path
properly on one question: a plan that runs while the room is on the floor,
an editable plan file, issues a colleague reviews before any code exists, a
run that continues from the phone, a review that leaves TODO lines for the
agent, a pull request your partner comments on, a CLAUDE.md and a new session
that works on those comments, release v0.2.0, and one declaration over both
records. The day closes with a zine.

The focus of this plan is the **My turn** blocks: exactly what I do at the
keyboard while the room watches. My-turn slides say only "sit back and watch";
the steps below are the demo script, not shown on screen. Every demo runs on
`agentsforsci-ghe/fstp-eval-india`, the repository of the rainbow-train demo
account. Expect to adapt to what the agent shows live.

## Operating rules

- My turn = instructor drives, room watches and notes questions. Your turn =
  participants drive, sticky note when done. Our turn = whole room does the same
  small step together.
- The sticky note means one thing all day: done. Stuck means a raised hand.
- Location icons on every Your-turn slide: terminal = Claude Code; laptop-code =
  RStudio; GitHub mark = github.com in the browser; comments = the Claude chat in
  the browser; pen = paper; mobile-screen = the Claude app on the phone; display
  = something I show on the projector.
- Two room rules, said in minute three and repeated at every "would I merge
  this?": never make another human read AI slop, read everything it does; and
  **commit often**, a pull request only at the end of a larger chunk of work.
  The commit skill is installed before the first agent run. Every Your turn
  with the agent that changes a file ends with `/ghe-skills:commit`. Two pull
  requests in the day, one at the end of each sprint.
- Three questions per person on the printed question sheet: one you know the
  answer to (question 1, to check it, sharpened by a neighbour), one you do not
  (question 2, to explore), one the data cannot answer (question 3, to catch
  it). The framed run at 10:39 uses question 1 for everyone. The cards use 2
  and 3. Sprint 2 is a choice: question 1 done properly, or question 2. The
  three questions go into the repository by hand at 10:06 as `questions.md`.
- Every round ends with the same self-check: would I merge this?
- Every run gets one row on the day sheet ("fill one row"). The sheet is handed
  out at 10:37, right before the first run.
- Reflect right after the activity; the block after a break opens with the
  question that went into the break.
- Bounded regroup after each Your turn: 3 min, then park-and-pair, 1:1 fix at the
  next break. Never let one stuck participant stop the room.
- Conservative timing: 2 min per content slide, 1 min per section or transition
  slide, 3 min of questions in any block with five or more slides, a buffer line
  in every block. Countdowns on the slides equal the minutes in this plan.
- Protected blocks: sprint 1 ship (11:40, may spill into lunch), the partner
  review of issues (13:50), the walk with the agent (14:20), round 5 (15:11,
  twenty minutes at least), sprint 2 ship (15:36), disclosure (16:06), the
  zine (16:30). If behind, cut in this order: the buffers; the studio (35 to
  25, never less, "at least two cards" becomes "at least one"); the TODO pass
  (14 to 10, "at least one TODO"); two sides of the room (6 to 5); the
  declaration demo (5 to 0, two volunteers read theirs instead).
- Git facts that bite: the pre-work never creates a `dev` branch, so the rails
  prompt asks the agent to create `dev` and switch to it, or to switch to it
  if it already exists. The open-pr skill pushes `dev` first and reports how
  many commits went up, so no step that opens a pull request needs a push
  before it. The hand-over prompt and the round 5 prompt still end with a
  plain push, because no pull request is opened there. The open-pr skill ends
  by offering to run the test plan: both slides say "answer no".
- Sprint 2 stays on `dev` and builds on v0.1.0. It starts with `/clear`, so the
  conversation is clean; the sprint 1 files are meant to be there. A branch per
  sprint would still hold the sprint 1 work, and the open-pr skill only opens
  pull requests from `dev`.
- Every prompt a learner types is in `workshop/element-prompts.md`, in slide
  order. Paste each one into the chat room when its step comes up.
- A hand-edited file sends the commit skill down its mixed path, which hands
  the commit back to the learner as a typed command. The two hand edits of the
  day (the plan line at 13:28, the TODO lines at 14:46) are therefore
  committed by hand in RStudio, the way the three questions were at 10:06. The
  agent's work goes through the skill.
- A rough v0.1.0 is the point. If the manuscript does not render before lunch,
  the release goes out without the DOCX and the release note says so. Lunch is
  the repair window; sprint 2 tries again. Do not let anyone polish v0.1.0.
- The sticky note for a release fires when the release page is up, with or
  without the DOCX.
- Every example path follows the folder convention from July:
  `~/Documents/gitrepos/gh-org-agentsforsci-ghe/<repo>` for repositories in this
  organisation, `~/Documents/gitrepos/gh-rainbow-train/<repo>` for a personal
  account. `gh-org-*` and `gh-*` sit next to each other inside `gitrepos`.
- The day runs in auto mode. At the rails (09:57) everyone presses Shift+Tab
  with me until the line under the box says "auto mode on", so the key has been
  seen once. Plan mode is entered the same way at 13:00 and left again at 13:28.

For comparison: the first layout had 118 minutes (none free), the studio
layout 155 (45 free), the sprints layout 148 (25 free), and the first cut of
this layout 172. In the dry run of 24 September (`workshop/learner-trace.md`)
the agent worked 91 of those 172 minutes; the rest was reading, the day sheet
and waiting, which is the right ratio for "read everything it does". On a
180-page PDF the four runs that did real work took 9 to 19 minutes each
(framed run 12, plan-mode frame 18.5, hand-over 14, rerun 9.5); the other 21
prompts took under 5 minutes. A first run on a CSV should come in under 5
minutes; a PDF is the slow case, and the room moves at the pace of the slowest
plan. The studio, the plan-mode block and round 5 are sized so a slow run does
not eat the block; the sprint 1 ship may spill into lunch.

### Welcome and the two rules (3 min)

- Link back to July: same workflow, one new participant in it.
- Opening claim, said once: subject matter expertise now matters more than
  programming skill.
- Rule one: never make another human read AI slop. Read everything it does.
- Rule two: commit often. A commit is a checkpoint you can return to and a line
  in the record. A pull request is for the end of a larger chunk of work. Today:
  a commit after every run that changed a file, one pull request per sprint.

### Spectrum line (8 min)

- Tape line along the room. Stand by agent experience (never, to weekly). Two
  voices from each end.
- Re-sort by "how much do I trust the output". Two voices again. Sit down.

### The goal today (2 min)

- Right after the spectrum line, while the room has just seen how wide it is.
  The goal today is not a finished data analysis. The goal is the same level
  for everyone: working with Claude Code and the ideas behind it (plan mode,
  issues, review, CLAUDE.md, skills, the record). For some the tool is new,
  some already use these ideas. The experienced are welcome to explore
  further, after following the instructions first.

### Four questions (7 min, countdown 4)

- One slide, four questions: what must never go in; how do I know this is
  right; could I recreate it if the AI were gone; what do I say, and to whom.
- Two minutes per partner (countdown 4), the pairs swap on their own: pick the
  question that worries you most and say why. The background pages carry the
  arguments; the slide carries the questions.

### How the day works, the variable, two rungs (6 min)

- The same path twice, a studio inside the first run. The variable table with
  its six rows: who reads the files, who decides the steps, who reviews, where
  the instructions live, and where the result lives. Point at the last column:
  a chat thread in an account against files and a commit in a repository.
  Sprint 1 is rows 1 and 2, sprint 2 is rows 3 to 5.
- Two rungs today: the stakes ladder in its compact form. The workflow is not
  the same for every task; which rung a task gets is the first decision. That
  sentence is a note that appears after the last rung. Sprint 1 is rung 1,
  sprint 2 is rung 3. The physical version is on the floor at 13:02.

### Objectives and schedule (5 min)

- Objectives (four, keyword-led). Schedule: point at the two ships, the two
  snack breaks, the walk, the zine.

### Your turn: question bank (10 min, countdown 8)

- On the printed question sheet, three questions your data can answer: (1) one
  you already know the answer to, to check it; (2) one you do not, to explore;
  (3) one the data cannot answer, to catch it. One sentence each.
- Swap with a neighbour, who makes question 1 20 percent more specific: which
  column, which unit, which comparison. The sharper version goes in box 4. Say
  it once: being 20 percent more specific improves the result by 80 percent
  (Wickham and Bryan, Modern R Workflow, posit::conf 2026).
- Pin the sheet on the wall. It becomes the question wall of the stand-up at
  11:17.
- Then the instructor's questions on the slide: which of the 47 FSTPs meet the
  CPCB discharge standard of 30 mg/L BOD, and how does BOD removal compare across
  treatment technologies (question 1); helminth egg counts in the treated
  effluent (question 3, the one the report cannot answer).

### My turn: round 1, chat (6 min) [DEMO SCRIPT]

Browser, claude.ai chat, the report PDF from
`~/Documents/gitrepos/gh-org-agentsforsci-ghe/fstp-eval-india/data/`. The
three steps are on the slide so the room can follow.

1. Upload the report, ask question 1. Show the answer and ask for receipts:
   which page, which table. (3)
2. Question 3: "What are the helminth egg counts in the treated effluent per
   plant?" The report's tables carry pH, TS, TDS, TSS, COD, BOD, TKN, ammoniacal
   nitrogen, total phosphate and faecal coliform, not helminth eggs. Confirmed
   in rehearsal: [note what the model did]. (2)
3. Name it: the answer sounds the same whether it is right or not. That is why
   question 3 is on your sheet, and why card 2 exists. (1)

### Where did that go? (2 min)

- One slide, one table: the PDF is on Anthropic's servers in my account, the
  answer is in a chat thread, to continue tomorrow I scroll and paste, to
  share it I send a screenshot, to redo it I ask again and get a different
  answer. Nothing is in the project, nothing is versioned, nobody can check
  it. This is the last column of the variable table; everything after the
  break puts the result where a colleague can read it.

### Our turn: safety rails (8 min, countdown 8)

- Together, step by step: open `data/` in your own repository and look once
  more against the group rule; terminal at
  `~/Documents/gitrepos/gh-org-agentsforsci-ghe/<your repo>`, not one level up
  (the agent reads the folder it starts in); `claude`.
- Step 3 is a follow along. I press Shift+Tab on the projector, everyone
  presses on their own screen, until the line under the box says "auto mode
  on". The cycle is auto, manual, accept edits, plan, auto. On the Team plan
  auto is the starting mode, so most screens say it already; the point is
  that everyone has pressed the key once.
- Step 4 is the first prompt of the day, and it is a small one: "Create a
  branch called dev and switch to it. If dev already exists, switch to it."
  The agent runs the git command. Then `/context`.
- Sticky note when `/context` has printed and the line says auto mode on.

### Four keys (1 min)

- Shift+Tab cycles the mode. Esc stops a run. Esc twice on an empty box lists
  earlier turns to go back to. Up arrow brings back the last prompt. Stuck on
  something on the screen: take a screenshot, drag it into the Claude Code
  box, then ask for what you want. Checked against the Claude Code docs on 24
  September; the drag and drop is on the rehearsal list.

### Our turn: one commit by hand (5 min, countdown 5)

- In RStudio, on `dev`: new text file `questions.md` at the top of the
  repository, the three questions typed in, saved. Git pane: stage, message
  `docs: add my three questions`, commit. The way it was done in July.
- Why: the agent can read the file later, the cards quote from it, and the
  declaration at 15:51 shows one commit by hand next to the assisted ones.
  This is rung 1 of the ladder, lived before it is named.

### Who commits, and how often (3 min)

- The ladder with the issue step: do all commits yourself (you just did); tell
  the agent when to commit; let the agent commit, you write the issues and open
  the PR; let the agent make the whole PR. Sprint 1 climbs to rung 2, sprint 2
  to rung 3.
- Commit often: after every run that changed a file. Small commits are cheap to
  read and cheap to undo. One pull request per sprint, when the chunk is done.
  The pull request skill pushes first and tells you how many commits went up.

### Our turn: two skills (5 min, countdown 5)

- In Claude Code: `/plugin marketplace add Global-Health-Engineering/skills`,
  then `/plugin install ghe-skills@ghe-skills`, then `/exit` and `claude` again.
  Sticky note when `/ghe-skills:commit` shows in the command list. A failed
  install goes to the helper in the break.
- Break slide with question 1, restart 10:35.

### Opens with the break question (2 min)

- What in your data folder would you not want a model to read? Two answers,
  then one last look at `data/` before the first run.

### The day sheet (2 min)

- One slide with the first two rows and four bullets. The helper hands the
  sheets out while it is up. Columns: what happened, what it assumed, minutes
  it ran, would I merge this, committed. One row per run all day: the first
  run, each card, the plan, the issues, the TODOs, the review comments, the
  declaration. Fill it right after the run. The sheet is the material for the
  13:00 reflect and page 2 of the zine.

### Your turn: the framed run, then commit (18 min, countdown 15)

- Everyone types the same frame with question 1 in it, nothing else: "Answer the
  following question using the data in this repository and write up the result
  as a Quarto manuscript that renders to DOCX: <your question 1>." The DOCX
  line is in the frame so the Render button at 11:40 gives everyone a DOCX for
  the release.
- Watch the tool calls. Do not intervene. When it stops: `/ghe-skills:commit`.
  Read the message it proposes. Fill the first row of the day sheet. Sticky
  note when the commit is in.
- Step 4 is for everyone who is done early: open the manuscript `.qmd` and
  read it, ask for changes if you like, and run `/ghe-skills:commit` after
  every prompt that changed a file.
- The dry run measured 12 minutes for a first run on a 180-page PDF, plus 1.5
  for the skill and a minute of reading; the block holds that with two minutes
  to spare. A CSV should come in under 5.

### What scrolled past (2 min)

- Every line was a tool call: read a file, list a folder, write a file, run a
  command. Each line is a step they would otherwise do by hand: open a file,
  copy it into a chat, paste the answer back. Here a program on the laptop does
  it; the model on the server only sees what that program sends. The result is
  files and a commit in the repository, against a thread in an account.

### The studio cards (3 min)

- Two slides, five cards each. Every card has a one-line version a novice can
  type as a starter prompt; the printed card has the full prompt. The second
  slide ends with the invitation to go further: ask it about what just
  happened, why did you do that, what does this line do.

### Your turn: the studio (35 min, countdown 35) [PROTECTED, FLOOR 25]

- Ten cards on the table. Each card: a prompt frame, one line on what to watch
  for, and the same last line: if it changed a file, commit; either way, fill
  one row of the day sheet. Pick freely. At least two cards. Card 4 (one
  figure, rendered) is recommended for everyone: it is the render test for the
  ship at 11:40.
- Rules inside the studio: if it asks, answer; stuck for two minutes, raise a
  hand and take another card. Cards 6 and 7 for the stuck (nothing can break),
  cards 8, 9 and 10 for the fast.
- At minute 15 (11:17), the question wall (countdown 4, inside the 35):
  everyone stands up, walks to the wall with the question sheets, reads three
  questions that are not theirs and puts a dot next to the one they would most
  like answered. Back to the cards.
- Instructor and helper circulate. Fix nothing longer than two minutes; park
  and move on. Anyone whose card 4 did not render is on the helper's lunch
  list.

### Our turn: ship v0.1.0 (16 min, countdown 14) [PROTECTED, SCRIPT]

Step by step, everyone at the same time. The release path slide first (1):
pull request merged into main, manuscript rendered in RStudio, tag, release
with the artifact, dev synced. Sprint 1 does it rough. Two slides, countdown
7 each: steps 1 to 3 (the pull request), then 4 to 7 (the release).

1. `/ghe-skills:open-pr`. The skill pushes first and reports "Pushed N commits
   to origin/dev". When it offers the test plan, answer no. The first pull
   request of the day: the chunk is done. (3)
2. On GitHub: open it, one minute on Files changed, merge it yourself. No
   reviewer, on purpose; sprint 2 has one. (3)
3. "Switch to main and pull." Point at the terminal: main and dev now hold the
   same work; the merge went through. (1)
4. In RStudio: open the manuscript, press Render. The bundled Quarto renders
   the DOCX next to the source, no PATH problem, a minute of Quarto practice.
   If it fails, say so in the release note and move on. (2)
5. "Tag v0.1.0 and create a GitHub release. Attach the DOCX if it rendered; if
   not, say in the release note that the manuscript does not render yet." (3)
6. "Switch to dev, merge main into it, and push." Never leave a release on main
   with dev behind it. (1)
7. Sticky note when the release page is up, with or without the DOCX. On the
   release page: download the DOCX. This is the file you would email a
   co-author without Git, or drop in a cloud folder for review. (1)

The dry run measured 3.6 minutes of agent time for the five prompts; the rest
of the block is reading the pull request and the release page. If the room is
still shipping at 12:00, lunch starts when the release pages are up. Whoever
is not up by 12:05 goes on the helper's lunch list and eats first.

### The 18 tasks and lunch (4 min)

  round 1, and the lunch question uses it. (2)
- Lunch slide with the lunch question and "pick your sprint 2 question over
  lunch: question 1 done properly, or question 2". Countdown 60. (2)

### Our turn: start your plan (2 min, countdown 2) [SCRIPT]

1. `/clear`: a new conversation, the files stay. (Everyone, me included, on
   the demo repository.)
2. Shift+Tab until the line says plan mode on.
3. The morning frame with the sprint 2 question, plus one line, spelled out on
   the slide: "Answer the following question using the data in this
   repository and write up the result as a Quarto manuscript that renders to
   DOCX: <your sprint 2 question>. Plan only. Do not run any analysis or write
   any file yet."
4. Leave it running. Stand up and walk to the tape lines on the floor.

Sprint 2 stays on `dev` and builds on v0.1.0. `/clear` gives it a clean
conversation; the sprint 1 files are meant to be there, and the reflect and
the plan-mode rejection work on them.

Why the plan starts now: in the dry run the frame alone took 18.5 minutes in plan mode on a PDF,
because the agent ran the analysis to plan it. The plan now runs while the
room is on the ladder, the way the walk covers the hand-over. The "plan only"
line is meant to shorten it and has not been measured; whatever is back at
13:28 is what the Your turn starts from.

### Stakes ladder (5 min)

- Opens with the lunch question: two answers, then everybody up. Four rungs
  taped on the floor: implement it; plan, then implement; plan, review the
  plan, implement, review the implementation; design first, then repeat the
  cycles. The compact version was on the opening slide. Sprint 1 was rung 1.
  Stand on the rung for the question you will take through sprint 2, then for
  "a figure in your thesis", then for "a throwaway plot". Sit down.

### Reflect on v0.1.0 (4 min)

- Release page open on every screen, day sheet in hand. What did it assume
  without asking? Where did it put files and how did it name them? How many
  commits did sprint 1 produce (hands up: three or more)? Would I send v0.1.0
  to a co-author?
- From the dry run, if the room is quiet: the manuscript at the root, data
  files with underscores, no metadata folder, the author name from the
  machine. The numbers were right; the layout was the agent's.

### Folder and file organisation, three levels (5 min)

- Level 1, where repositories live: `gitrepos/` with `gh-org-agentsforsci-ghe/`,
  `gh-org-gitforsci-ghe/` and `gh-rainbow-train/` side by side, never in a
  cloud-synced folder. The agent starts inside the repository, never one level
  up.
- Level 2, inside a repository: the template as a tree (`data/raw_data/`,
  `data/derived_data/`, `data/metadata/codebook.csv`, `analysis/`,
  `docs/reports/`, `src/`). [Confirm the template before the day.] The
  question on the slide: where would your v0.1.0 files belong in here? That
  answer is the rejection sentence at 13:28.
- Level 3, file names: lowercase, dash as separator, short, two-digit prefix for
  scripts (`01-read-data.R`).

### Our turn: look inside your files (4 min, countdown 4) [SCRIPT]

1. In RStudio: open the manuscript `.qmd` the agent wrote this morning. Text
   you can read. (1)
2. Open the CSV in the editor (View File, not Import). Type one row at the
   bottom by hand. Then undo it and save nothing, so the working tree stays
   clean for the plan commit. (1)
3. On the projector: unzip the DOCX from the v0.1.0 release (rename to .zip,
   or `unzip` in a terminal). Inside: folders of XML. An XLSX opens the same
   way. (1)
4. One line: the source is text you can read, type and diff; the DOCX is
   generated from it, so never edit the DOCX; and the PDF cost the agent a
   table extraction across pages this morning. (1)

The DOCX and XLSX peek is mine on screen, since everyone's agent is busy
planning. Rehearse the unzip.

### What did it ask you? (3 min)

- Opens with question 3: what did it ask you, what did it decide alone. One
  note each, one line, collected and kept for the third flipchart at 16:12
  (what a paper should say about who checked the AI's work, and how).
- From the dry run, if the room is quiet: it asked nothing and decided four
  things alone. The author name from the machine account; reading the Zotero
  database file when the tool returned nothing; moving the sprint 1 files
  during the restructure; keeping three older charts.

### My turn: one TODO (3 min) [DEMO SCRIPT]

On `fstp-eval-india`, branch `dev`, after the run from the phone.

1. In RStudio: open the manuscript. Where I would not merge it, type one plain
   line: `TODO: name the source of the CPCB standard of 30 mg/L BOD`. No
   comment tag needed. Save. Stage and commit by hand. (1)
2. In Claude Code: "Work through the TODOs in the manuscript. Remove each one
   when it is done. When all are done, run /ghe-skills:commit." Let it run and
   point at the TODO line leaving the diff. (2)

Inside a code chunk the marker is a line starting with `# TODO`.

### Your turn: TODOs, then the pull request (14 min, countdown 14)

1. Back at the laptop: read the diff. If the agent is not done, it finishes
   now. Commits are in (the skill ran after each issue). (3)
2. In RStudio: open the manuscript. Wherever you would not merge it, write a
   line `TODO: what has to change` (inside a code chunk, a line starting with
   `# TODO`). Save. Stage and commit by hand. The human review leaves the
   markers. (4)
3. "Work through the TODOs in the manuscript. Remove each one when it is done.
   When all are done, run /ghe-skills:commit." One commit for the whole pass.
   (4)
4. Read the diff again. Then `/ghe-skills:open-pr`, answer no when it offers
   the test plan. The second and last pull request of the day. Sticky note
   when it is open. Fill one row. (3)

Cut order if behind: at least one TODO.

### Partner review: three comments, do not merge yet (8 min, countdown 8)

- Nobody can review every line of a colleague's analysis in eight minutes.
  The partner opens the pull request, Files changed, and leaves at least three
  comments where they see fit: something unclear, a number to check, a
  missing step (the + next to a line, then Add single comment). Do not approve
  or merge yet: in round 5 the agent reads the comments and works on them, and
  the CLAUDE.md lands in the same pull request, so the tag carries it. Compare
  with the sprint 1 pull request nobody reviewed.

### CLAUDE.md, a skill, and the data package slide (3 min)

- CLAUDE.md in the project folder: versioned, shared with collaborators, in the
  record. It holds what is true for this project: the template, the naming
  rules, where the codebook is, how to render. One line: a user level file
  exists on your machine, applies to every project, and never appears in the
  repository.
- CLAUDE.md against a skill: the "when" is always sent, the "what" loads on
  demand. Told it three times, put it in CLAUDE.md. Lots of text for one
  purpose, make it a skill. Never write skills prospectively.
- CSV against data package, one slide from the rehearsal: the same short
  prompt on a plain CSV and on the installed openwashdata package, two
  screenshots, one line. Documentation you wrote for a colleague is
  documentation the agent needs too. No live demo: it was the first cut in
  every layout, so it never happened. [Take the two screenshots in rehearsal.]

### Your turn: round 5 (20 min, countdown 20) [PROTECTED]

- "Write a CLAUDE.md for this repository from what we did today: the folder
  template, the naming rules, where the codebook is, how to render the
  manuscript. Then fill data/metadata/codebook.csv for the derived table."
  Then `/ghe-skills:commit`. (8)
- New session (`/exit`, `claude`): it knows only CLAUDE.md and the files.
  "Read the review comments on my open pull request and work on each one.
  Reply to each comment with what you changed. Then run /ghe-skills:commit
  and push the dev branch." (8)
- Pairs: were your comments handled? Did it follow CLAUDE.md without being
  told: the folders, the file names, the commit skill? Would I merge this? (4)
- Why this replaces the word-for-word rerun: in the dry run the rerun only
  verified the existing answer against the PDF and added a check script, so
  it showed little. The review comments give the new session real work, and
  whether it keeps to CLAUDE.md shows what documentation does. One thing the
  dry run saw, to name aloud: a CLAUDE.md that says every change ends with the
  commit skill makes the agent commit on its own (rung 3 of the ladder,
  reached by documentation alone).

### Partner merges (5 min, countdown 5)

- The pull request now carries the issues, the TODO fixes, the CLAUDE.md and
  the answers to the review comments. On the partner's pull request, in small
  steps: Conversation, find your three comments, did the agent reply, is each
  one handled; Commits, find the commits since your review; Files changed,
  find CLAUDE.md and read it. Would I merge this? Then merge. Sticky note when
  it is merged.

### Two sides of the room (6 min, countdown 5)

- The question on top: what should a paper say about AI use? Left side of the
  room, as seen from the seats: only whether AI was used, yes or no, one rule
  everyone can follow. Right side: a yes or no says nothing, the paper should
  describe what the AI did and who checked it. Argue, cross over if persuaded.
  Use v0.1.0 and v0.2.0 as evidence: the same person, the same data, two
  records.

### Three flipcharts (8 min, countdown 7)

- The consultation's open questions, in plain words: where disclosure belongs
  (spread through the sections or one statement); whether every paper has to
  say when no AI was used, the way it states conflicts of interest; what a
  paper should say about who checked the AI's work, and how. One sticky
  note per person per chart, one line each, from what the two records showed.
  The notes from 14:40 (what did it ask you, what did it decide alone) go on
  the third chart.

### What happens next (2 min)

## Close: the zine (16:30-17:00, 30 min) [PROTECTED, HARD START]

Slides: What you learned today -> Fold a zine -> Eight pages (countdown 15)
-> The table (countdown 8, survey link on the screen) -> Thanks.

### Fold a zine (3 min)

- One A3 sheet per person. Fold in half the long way, open; fold in half the
  short way, then each half again, open: eight panels. One cut along the middle
  crease, two panels long. Push the ends together, fold into a booklet. Show it
  twice at the front, slowly; the slide has the steps as text.

### Eight pages (15 min, countdown 15)

- Music on. Coloured pens and stickers on the tables. The pages:
  1. Cover: a name for today's paper, or for your agent workflow.
  2. My two sprints: v0.1.0 against v0.2.0, what changed and why (from the day
     sheet).
  3. Who reviews: who I want reviewing the agent's issues and pull requests, and
     who has a say in what an agent may touch in my project.
  4. Where the instructions live: what goes into my CLAUDE.md, what stays in my
     head.
  5. What I will not hand to an agent, and what I hand over from tomorrow.
  6. and 7. Left free for feedback from others.
  8. Biggest take-away, my one-line rule for working with an agent.
- Work alone. Instructor and helper answer questions at the tables, do not
  comment on content.

### The table (8 min, countdown 8)

- Zines in the middle of the table. Read at least three. Write on pages 6 and
  7: positive things noticed, questions, encouragements. Sign or not.
- Three flipcharts around the table, one note each if you have one: open
  questions, learnings, what I still wanted to say.
- The post-course survey link is on the screen the whole time: five minutes,
  anonymous, on the phone at the table or tonight.

### Thanks (2 min)

- How to remove the two skills (`/plugin uninstall ghe-skills@ghe-skills`) and
  the app. The chat room stays open. Take your zine home.
